questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: In the process of choosing a destination, I was looking for a university with a good research profile that fits my academic interest. At the same time, I wanted to improve my English and be in a region that also interests me culturally. The Bay Area seemed like the perfect place for that.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. KU and Berkeley had many resouces available and were easy to reach in case I had questions. The Berkeley International Office kind of spams you with information, so it's hard to miss the important things. All communtication was quick and uncomplicated. The COVID regulations were a bit confusing as it was not sure if and how the States would let students in, but that's due to the unpredicable nature of the pandemic. The international office tried their best to give all the support I needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I used the resources available on the Berkeley International Office website. The mandatory Golden Bear Orientation week is supposed to provide new students with all information they need. I didn't attend because I got COVID, but also felt that at that time I already knew everything I needed for the start of the semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Housing is expensive in the Bay Area, but it is not hard to find. Just make sure you don't get scamed. I'd recommend to see the apartment in person before you sign the lease if it's not one of the official university accomodations (Some people I met had really bad experiences with apartments they didn't see in person beforehand).
For the first semester, I moved into an apartment with 2 students I met on Cal Rentals, the official university housing network. You'll get an invitation from the university which has the advantage that there should almost be no scam on this platform.
For the second semester I moved into one of the co-ops (
https://bsc.coop/
). These are self-administered alternative student houses in Berkeley that arguably offer the cheapest rent around here. Honestly, I had the best time here and I can highly recommend this option as it gives you a great opportunity to meet many cool people (outside the international bubble!) and have a great time. Once you're in a co-op, you'll meet not only your house mates, but many folks from other houses as well. I think all other options are more expensive.
I-House would be another option almost exclusively for international students. I think it's extremely overpriced (like the other on-campus dorms) and keeps you mostly with (mainly wealthy) exchange student, which I decided was nothing for me. However, they have a great community and I think you could definitely have a great time there if that's what you like.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: For the co-ops make sure you get on their wait list asap, right after you get your acceptance (or even before if you are confident). As an exchange student you'll be placed before the new students, so you'll have a good chance of getting a spot if you're on the list early! Even if you don't get a spot right away there still might be spots opening up throughout the summer as some people cancel late.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The registration was straigt forward, however returning students are prioritized in the course selection, and if the class belongs to a certain major, these students could be prioritized as well. This means that there's the chance that courses are full before exchange students are able to select them. It is possible to be placed on a wait list, but with uncertain prospect of success.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Classes are selected in Cal Central, the univerity's course system. A course catalog is available on the Berkeley website too, including all necessary information.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Everythin should be covered in GBO and in the mails sent out by BIO and the university.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Many classes I wanted to take were full when it was my turn to select. I had to be flexible, but in the end I ended up with classes I was interested in.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Select you classes as early as possible. It's a good idea to have a list of classes prepared beforehand, which gives you some flexibility in case courses are full. Don't waste your time on long waitlists.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Berkeley has a high academic profile with many professors being leaders of their fields. Sitting in their lecures and office hours is abolutely amazing. Make sure to check on
ratemyprofessors.com/
beforehand.
I came to the US as a master student, however, UCEAP requires you to be undergrad. This is fine as the american undergrad is 4 years instead of 3. However that means you're restricted to undergrad classes with max. 1 grad class per semester (which has to be approved by the professor in advance). I mainly choose cross-listed classes for both upper-division undergrad and grad students. For my second semester I did research for my master's thesis in a group at Berkeley and enrolled for that in full-time research units. This was a great experience, as I was able to be part of a world-class research team and will continue working with them on some projects. It is important to contact the UCPH and Berkeley advisors in advance to make sure this is accepted by everyone. Also for bachelor students, professors offer research units (URAP), which is a great way to experience world-class research.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of classes is similar to the ones in CPH but the workload is very high. I recommend taking as few classes as possible to not be burried in assignments for the entire stay. Many Berkeley students are stressed-out by the high workload and put a lot of pressure on themselves to perform well in the classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The lecures themselves are less personal than in CPH, but the contact to the professors is very casual. Many of them offer office hours which are great to talk about the materials, homework, or their research, and many of them offer to talk about personal issues too. The classes I had were structured into lecture, tutorial, and office hours and included weekly or bi-weekly assignments.
Classes go for one semester with mid-terms and finals. Together with the scores on the assignments they determine the final grades.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Carbon Cycle Dynamics
Geo-Information Systems
Individual Research on Remote Sensing
Chamber Chorus

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer: Individual Graduate Research (Keenan Group)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Carbon Cycle Dynamics was a great choice. It's taught by Inez Fung, who is one of the leading scientists in that field and one of Joe Biden's scientific advisors. Listening to her personal stories gave me a great insight in how the climate science community works and how it's connected to politics and economy. In her office hours we had great discussions about many climate change related topics.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
The University tries to force students into their SHIP health insurance program. This is complete non-sense, as it offers the same as other insurances at an exorbitant price. SHIP can be waived with an insurance that complies with the university's standards. I waived it with the cheapest insurance I could find on
https://www.isoa.org/
and just in case got a european international insurance on top (which is not accepted for the waiver, but covers more than ISO). Through that I could save a lot of money even though I technically was covered by 2 insurances.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The prices are kind of similar, if not a little higher than in Europe. Housing is extremely expensive. The local transit (in the east-bay region) is free for Berkeley students. Also, the basic needs center hands out free food supplies once a week, which is another way to reduces costs if needed.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Literally everyting you can think of. Some societies are very sought after at it can be that you have to pass several rounds of interviews to be accepted (mostly for business clubs).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Getting involved in one of the many clubs at Berkeley is a good way to meet people and get involved in the unique campus culture in Berkeley. I joined the chamber chorus and took some DeCal classes in Swing dance.
I also can highlý recommend joining the CHAOS outdoor club (
https://www.chaosberkeley.org/
). They organize many get-togethers and hikes, which is a great way to meet people in the beginning. For a one-time fee of 10$, you'll ge access to their gear shed where you can take any equipment you need for your travels (and they have a lot!).

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Get to know the Bay Area and everything that's around it, such as Yosemite NP, Kings Canyon NP, Sequoia NP, Lassen NP, Point Reyes, Santa Cruz, Big Sur, ... There's a lot to see!
Californians are very outdoorsy, so its never a probem to get good recommendations and travel buddies. And as I said, the outdoor club might do the trick...

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I feel in many ways the american culture is not so different from the European (at least it's still a "western" society).

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I found friends in the co-ops, GBO, courses, and in the societies I joined on campus. Many students are open-minded and it is easy to make first contact. Despite the cliche that many americans seem superficial at first, I found people I'm sure I'm gonna stay in contact with beyond my stay abroad.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Berkeley and the Bay Area in general is in a severe housing crisis, which results in many people living on the streets. For someone coming from a country with a working social system and healthcare, it is shocking to see how big the gap between poor and rich is in the US and especially here in the Bay. Going to Berkeley sometimes seemed like being in the proverbial Ivory Tower, as the university provides good oportunities for their students, but massively contributes to the housing shortage in the city.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Berkeley probably is the most tolerant and diverse place i've seen so far. It's great to see how the university and the student body tries to fight discrimination as much as possible. This stands very much in contrast to many other regions in the US.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Be fast and do things ASAP (housing, visa, tickets, etc)
2) Join clubs and societies to find people you like (and get out of the international bubble)
3) Don't let yourself be dragged into the stressed-out Berkeley mentality

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Bring warm clothes. Berkeley and especially SF is colder then you think!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being part of this amazing campus culture with all the traditions that I thought would only exist in the movies, and at the same time getting to know so many people with such a positive spirit who want to do something about the world's problems.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I had some trouble finding the right people in the beginning, as I had covid during the onboarding week and could not take part in the social activities. That, however, improved shortly after the beginning of the semester.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
